summary: Initial discovery for compatibility and eval sprint. Opal currently uses OpenAI for prod, vLLM for local fast inference, and TGI in a small experimental service. Main goals: verify eval parity on key prompts, understand latency/cost targets, evaluate Dedicated vs Private for data residency and compliance. Security questions (KMS, audit logs, RBAC) surfaced. Agreed to run benchmarks with Redwood-hosted and Dedicated trial capacity next week.
topics: deployment options: hosted vs dedicated vs private
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-30
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Recording: yes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood CSM), Jordan Lee (Opal CTO), Maya Chen (Opal ML), Samir Patel (Opal Security), Rita Gomez (Opal Product)

Auto-summary: quick alignment on goals + action items to run eval sprint, collect prompts + security docs.

---- Transcript ----
00:00 Alex Kim: hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Alex with Redwood, i'll do a quick run of the agenda, priya's gonna cover the technical bits.
00:12 Jordan Lee: hey thanks, yeah we have about an hour, um Jordan here from Opal. quick context, we run customer-facing summarization and policy matchers, prod is OpenAI right now but we have local inference via v-l-m for some latency-sensitive routes.
00:26 Maya Chen: and we tried T G I for a pilot, results were OK but there were quantization / tokenization quirks we need to evaluate more.
00:35 Priya Rao: cool, that's exactly the kind of mix we see. our goal today is to map your evaluation criteria, the prompt set, any perf baselines, and talk about deployment constraints — particularly data residency and KMS.
00:47 Rita Gomez: timeline wise we're aiming to pick a vendor for the q4 sprint, so relatively quick. cost is a hard requirement; latency under 200ms p50 for certain routes is ideal.
01:00 Samir Patel: from security, we need SOC2, ISO mention, audit logs, SSO/SAML, and whether keys live in our KMS or Redwood's. also retention policies, and VPC peering for private deploy is something we might require.
01:20 Alex Kim: understood. quick question: for your vLLM runs, are you using open-source weights or a hosted model? and are you doing quantization like 4-bit?
01:30 Maya Chen: we run a trimmed Llama-like model locally, quantized to int4 with bitsandbytes, and v-l-m orchestrates it. For some routes we call OpenAI's gpt w/ensemble fallback.
01:43 Priya Rao: ok makes sense. one thing to expect is parity differences — small prompt engineering changes can shift outputs. our eval sprint tries to measure Delta on your golden prompts and flags regressions.
01:58 Jordan Lee: what about tokenization differences? we saw mismatches when moving between the provider tokenizers — role tokens and special tokens were off.
02:10 Priya Rao: yes tokenizers matter — we run a tokenizer compatibility step. sometimes remapping special tokens or normalizing whitespace fixes most diffs. we'll include that in the prep checklist.
02:25 Alex Kim: could we talk hosting modes briefly — hosted vs dedicated vs private? sounds like security needs might push you to dedicated or private.
02:32 Samir Patel: private is preferred if we can't have keys in Redwood. We also want audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.
02:40 Priya Rao: for private deployments we can support customer-managed KMS and log ingestion to your Splunk/Datadog. Dedicated (reserved capacity) gives isolation without full private control plane. The trade is management surface vs speed to ship.
02:56 Maya Chen: curious on perf: for our quantized models we see kv cache IO issues. does Redwood support efficient KV cache warmups for short-lived sessions?
03:10 Priya Rao: yes we have continuous batching and KV cache warming heuristics; we can pin model variants with prewarmed caches for canaries. we'll show numbers in the benchmark.
03:25 Jordan Lee: pricing — how do you price for dedicated? we have steady throughput but bursty spikes.
03:33 Alex Kim: dedicated is reserved commit + burst credits. we'll run math against your CSV. For hosted, it's usage per token with tier discounts for committed spend.
03:45 Maya Chen: one tricky bit: our eval set includes long-context docs, 8k tokens typically. Any known perf cliffs at that length?
03:58 Priya Rao: at 8k we select kernels that are optimized for long attention; quantized path can still have a bit of overhead but it's predictable. we'll capture p50/p95/p99 in the stress run.
04:12 Rita Gomez: success criteria — besides latency and cost, we care about output quality. if Redwood passes our golden prompt suite with >95% parity on acceptance metrics, it's a pass.
04:26 Priya Rao: perfect, we'll design the acceptance checks and compute automatic regression alerts.
04:34 Jordan Lee: any competitors you see us considering that we should think about?
04:38 Alex Kim: you mentioned OpenAI & Anthropic already; some teams look at MosaicML or self-hosted v-l-m with orchestration. the key diff is operational burden and observability.
04:50 Samir Patel: about compliance, can you provide SOC2 artifact and point someone to your security questionnaire?
04:56 Lena Ortiz: yes we'll send the security pack, priya will attach it.
05:02 Maya Chen: for the benchmark, can Redwood run both hosted and a small dedicated cluster so we can compare outputs? ideally same model weights.
05:12 Priya Rao: absolutely — we can spin a short-lived dedicated pool for the run. we can also run local conversion tooling to ensure the same weight format between your v-l-m and our runtime. occasional conversion drift occurs, we'll surface diffs.
05:28 Jordan Lee: good. what's the typical time to spin a dedicated test cluster?
05:32 Alex Kim: usually 24-48 hours to provision test capacity and get it warmed.
05:37 Rita Gomez: ok timeline aligns. next steps?
05:40 Alex Kim: quick recap: Redwood to share security docs and KMS integration notes; Maya to upload eval set + current cost sheet; Redwood to schedule benchmark and quote dedicated trial; set calendar for a 3-hour slot next week for the run.
05:55 Jordan Lee: sounds good. one last question — does Redwood's runtime support tool-calling or function calling patterns we use for structured outputs?
06:04 Priya Rao: yes function/tool calling is supported; we have structured output and schema enforcement layers. small caveat when using quantized models — some parsing edgecases, but we handle via postprocess validators.
06:22 Samir Patel: about data retention — can you commit to per-customer retention settings and optional auto-delete after 30/90 days?
06:32 Alex Kim: yes per-customer retention policies are supported; for private deployments it's fully customer-controlled.
06:40 Rita Gomez: great, appreciate it.
06:44 Alex Kim: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and calendar invite.
06:49 Jordan Lee: thanks all.
06:52 Meeting end.

Notes on transcript quality: speaker overlaps and accents cause minor mislabels, some product names like vLLM recorded as "v-l-m" and TGI as "T G I" in places.
questions: Can Redwood run both hosted and dedicated benchmarks on identical weights?
How does Redwood handle KMS and customer-managed keys?
What is the expected provisioning time for dedicated test capacity?
How do tokenizers differences get normalized during eval?
